title: Green Chemistry
objective: After this level you can explain how chemists make processes safer and cleaner.
summary: Green chemistry designs out hazardous substances instead of cleaning them up later. Atom economy keeps starting materials in the product, as in a three-step ibuprofen route.

cards.headline: The cleanest way to handle hazardous waste? Never make it.
cards.body: That's the idea behind green chemistry. It changes the question from "How do we clean this up?" to "Why are we making it at all?"

cards.headline: Prevent, don't mop up
cards.body: Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use or generation of hazardous substances. That's different from cleanup, which treats waste after it's made, often by separating hazardous chemicals from everything else: a Level 7 job, on an industrial scale. Green chemistry works upstream, so there's less to separate in the first place.
cards.callout: Cleanup treats waste after it's made. Green chemistry avoids making it.

cards.headline: Twelve principles, starting with waste
cards.body: In 1998 Paul Anastas and John Warner set out the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry. The first: it's better to prevent waste than to treat or clean it up afterward. The second is atom economy: design reactions so the final product contains as much of the starting materials as possible. Picture a recipe where most of the ingredients go in the bin instead of the cake (an analogy). Atom economy keeps them in the cake.

cards.headline: The ibuprofen fix
cards.body: An older way of making ibuprofen, the everyday painkiller, took six steps, and under 40 percent of the atoms used ended up in the product. BHC Company found a route with three steps and about 80 percent. It also recovers and reuses its main byproduct. In 1997 the route won a US Presidential Green Chemistry Challenge Award.

cards.headline: Green chemistry: designed
learned: Green chemistry prevents hazardous substances instead of cleaning them up
Anastas and Warner's 12 principles (1998) start with preventing waste
Atom economy keeps starting materials in the product

questions.prompt: What does the green chemistry principle of atom economy aim for?

options.label: Using as few atoms as possible, whatever the product
options.rationale: The aim is where the atoms end up, not how few you use.

options.label: A product that keeps as much of the starting materials as possible
Making every reaction in the process run as fast as possible
Recycling products once people have finished using them
options.rationale: Atom economy is about the reaction itself.

questions.explanation: Atom economy means designing syntheses so the product keeps the maximum share of the starting materials, wasting few atoms.

questions.prompt: A factory makes a hazardous byproduct, then separates it out and treats it. Why isn't that green chemistry?

options.label: Green chemistry only applies to plants and farms
options.rationale: It applies to all areas of chemistry.

options.label: Treating waste after it's made is always illegal
options.rationale: Cleanup is legal and often necessary; it's just a different approach.

options.label: Green chemistry avoids making the hazard at all
Separating chemicals from waste is impossible
options.rationale: Separation is a routine part of cleanup.

questions.explanation: Cleanup deals with hazardous waste after it's made; green chemistry designs the process so it isn't made.

questions.prompt: Level 52 says no matter is lost in a reaction. In the old six-step ibuprofen route, where did most of the atoms used end up?

options.label: They were destroyed during the six steps
Outside the product, as other substances
Inside the ibuprofen, as extra weight
options.rationale: Under 40 percent of them made it into the product.

options.label: They turned into energy and heat
options.rationale: Atoms are rearranged, not turned into energy.

questions.explanation: Under 40 percent of the atoms used ended up in ibuprofen, so the rest left as other substances: poor atom economy.
